claims.text: The nanoparticles are initially solid, homogeneous high-entropy alloys containing iron, nickel, chromium, cobalt, and copper.
Local atomic-scale bonding heterogeneity and short-range-order variations occur in the nanoparticles.
Chemical complexity produces slight compositional clustering and local strain fields.
The constituent metals differ in atomic radii and bonding preferences.
Differences in atomic radii and bonding preferences make regions with slight compositional fluctuations thermodynamically less stable.
Compositionally fluctuating, strained regions nucleate local disorder and melting at lower temperatures than the rest of the particle.
Spatially heterogeneous liquid nucleation broadens the melting transition.
Preventing oxidation and extrinsic reactions ensures that observed thermal changes are intrinsic to the nanoparticles.
Single-metal or chemically simpler alloy nanoparticles provide a baseline with narrow, well-defined melting transitions and minimal localized premelting.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will begin premelting earlier in localized regions.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting interval.
The high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit multiple, less uniform exothermic calorimetric transitions.
The proposed mechanism applies to chemically complex nanoparticles that retain well-mixed solid-solution phases.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to significantly phase-separated systems.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to one- or two-element particles because their chemical uniformity is higher.
The magnitude of the temperature shift and the spatial distribution of premelting regions are uncertain.
A melting transition as sharp and spatially uniform as the baseline, with no earlier or heterogeneous premelting, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome describes multiple exothermic calorimetric transitions, whereas the proposed DSC measurement refers to the broadness and shape of a melting endotherm. The sign and thermal event being predicted are therefore inconsistent.
